choices.text: It shows no solved example of the task
choices.why: Right. The instruction and the input, and nothing worked through.

choices.text: It is sent at temperature 0
choices.why: Temperature is a sampling setting, lesson 13. Zero-shot is about what the prompt contains.

choices.text: It has to be answered in a single attempt
choices.why: The number of attempts has nothing to do with it. A zero-shot prompt can be retried.

choices.text: It gives the model no instruction at all, only the input text
choices.why: There is always an instruction. What is missing is a worked example.

prompt: The weak prompt was given `Do you open on public holidays?` and the reply answered the question. Why is that the expected result?
hint: What had the prompt said about messages that are not reviews?

choices.text: The model misread the question it was given
choices.why: It read it correctly, and did what questions usually call for.

choices.text: Temperature was too high
choices.why: Nothing about randomness explains a reply that is the most likely one.

choices.text: The model refused the task
choices.why: It did not refuse. It did a different task, one the prompt left open.

choices.text: Nothing said it might not be a review
choices.why: Right. Answering questions is what a chat model is trained to do; only the prompt could have said otherwise.

prompt: Which of these did the strong prompt add? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A definition for each of the four labels
choices.why: Yes: a clear task, including `mixed`, where two readers are likeliest to disagree.

choices.text: The message between `<message>` tags
choices.why: Yes: the input delimited, as in lesson 18.

choices.text: Two solved examples of messages and their labels
choices.why: That would make it few-shot, lesson 21. The strong prompt has none.

choices.text: A rule for sarcasm, other languages and questions
choices.why: Yes: the edge cases named.

prompt: Why does the strong prompt say "Sarcasm counts as what the writer means" when the model already knows what sarcasm is?
hint: Knowing what something is, against knowing what you want done with it.

choices.text: It teaches the model what sarcasm is
choices.why: The model learnt that in training. The sentence adds a decision, not knowledge.

choices.text: It records your choice of label, which the model cannot guess
choices.why: Right. The model knows sarcasm; it does not know whether the café files it by the words or the meaning.

choices.text: It makes the reply shorter
choices.why: It affects which label comes back, not the length of the reply.

choices.text: Models refuse to label sarcasm unless told to
choices.why: Nothing suggests a refusal. Without the rule the model labels it one way or the other.

prompt: Where do you find the edge cases a prompt should name?
hint: Not by thinking hard in advance.

choices.text: In the model's documentation
choices.why: Documentation describes the model, not the café's messages.

choices.text: In real inputs, labelled by hand
choices.why: Right. Every place two people disagree on a label is a sentence the prompt needs.

choices.text: By asking the model which inputs it finds hard
choices.why: A model's account of itself is not evidence, lesson 5.

choices.text: In a list of edge cases that applies to every task
choices.why: Edge cases belong to the task and its inputs; sarcasm matters here, and would not in a translation.

prompt: The strong prompt wraps what the customer wrote in tags so that the ___ is delimited from the instruction.
hint: One of the four fixes: the instruction and the ___.

prompt: What is a test set, in this lesson?

choices.text: The inputs a model scored highest on
choices.why: Nobody scored the inputs. The labels came first, from a person.

choices.text: Every message the café ever received
choices.why: Eight lines, chosen on purpose. Size is less important than coverage.

choices.text: The replies a model gave last time
choices.why: Those are what gets scored, not what it is scored against.

choices.text: Inputs with labels a person decided beforehand
choices.why: Right. The prompt's replies are compared with those labels and counted.

prompt: How many of the eight did the weak prompt's replies get right?
hint: The last line of the first `score.py` run.

prompt: `r1` was labelled `Positive!` by the weak prompt's reply. Why does `score.py` count it wrong when a person would count it right?
hint: Compare the two strings character by character.

choices.text: The review was not positive
choices.why: It was. The label's meaning is right; its form is not.

choices.text: `score.py` has a bug
choices.why: It compares exactly, which is what a program using the label would do.

choices.text: `Positive!` is not the string `positive`
choices.why: Right. The capital and the exclamation mark make it a different string. The prompt never stated the form of the answer.

choices.text: Exclamation marks are banned in JSON
choices.why: There is no JSON here. The test compares plain strings.

prompt: The strong prompt names sarcasm and still misses `r5`. What does the lesson suggest next?
hint: The table of failures and next moves.

choices.text: Describe sarcasm at greater length
choices.why: More of what did not work is the least likely fix. The table points to examples.

choices.text: Show it: an example with its label, lesson 21
choices.why: Right. A named edge case that is still missed is where examples show the boundary better than a description.

choices.text: Remove `r5` from the test set so the score is clean
choices.why: The test set is the evidence. Removing an inconvenient line hides the failure.

choices.text: Retrieve the café's handbook into the prompt
choices.why: Retrieval supplies facts. Sarcasm is not a missing fact.

prompt: With eight messages in the test set, by how many percentage points does one more miss change the score?
hint: One in eight, as a percentage.

prompt: A colleague tries the weak prompt on three glowing reviews, gets `positive` each time, and says it works. What is wrong with that test?
hint: What kinds of message did the three cover?

choices.text: Three is too few to compute a percentage
choices.why: A percentage of three is computable. The problem is what the three contain.

choices.text: Glowing reviews confuse models
choices.why: They are the easiest case there is, which is the problem.

choices.text: The colleague should have used temperature 0
choices.why: That changes the variability of replies, not what the test covers.

choices.text: It holds only easy cases
choices.why: Right. Inputs that any prompt handles score every prompt well. The test set needs mixed, sarcastic, foreign and non-review messages.

prompt: You add `r1` to `r8` to the prompt as examples, run the test set again and get 8 of 8. What does that score show?
hint: Where did the examples come from?

choices.text: That few-shot prompting is better than zero-shot
choices.why: It may be, but this score cannot show it. The test needs messages the prompt has not seen.

choices.text: That the model learnt the labels permanently
choices.why: A prompt changes nothing in the model. Remove the examples and the score drops back.

choices.text: That the test set was too easy all along
choices.why: The same set gave 3 and 7 before. The examples, not the set, explain the 8.

choices.text: Little: the test now contains the answers
choices.why: Right. The examples became the test, so the score measures recall of the prompt, not how it labels new messages.

prompt: Put the work of improving a zero-shot prompt in order.
hint: The labels come before any prompt is run.
items: Label a set of real inputs by hand
Run the prompt on them and count
Change the prompt for the commonest kind and count again

prompt: Match each failure from the weak prompt's replies to the fix that addresses it.

pairs.left: an answer to the customer's question
pairs.right: name non-reviews as an edge case
say which language the labels are in

prompt: When is a zero-shot prompt enough?

choices.text: When it meets the bar you set on the test set
choices.why: Right. The count decides against a bar chosen before running it.

choices.text: When the replies read well to you on a first look through them
choices.why: Reading well is what the weak prompt's replies did to a person, and three of eight were right.

choices.text: When the model says it understood the task
choices.why: A model's statement about its own understanding is not a measurement.

choices.text: When it has no spelling mistakes
choices.why: Spelling is not the bar. Correct labels on the test set are.

prompt: A zero-shot prompt asks for the café's Wi-Fi password and the model gives a confident wrong one. Which move from the lesson's table applies?
hint: Is this a format, an edge case, or a fact?

choices.text: Supply the facts: context or retrieval, lessons 24 and 11
choices.why: Right. No wording of the instruction gives the model a fact it does not have.

choices.text: Name it as an edge case
choices.why: Naming a case makes a decision. It does not supply a password.

choices.text: State the output format
choices.why: The format was fine; the content was wrong.

choices.text: Add a few examples of Wi-Fi passwords so the model sees the pattern
choices.why: Examples show a pattern, not the café's actual network. Note also that the staff network's name is never given to guests.
